# The coolant is boiling when I shut off engine

When you hear a bubbling or boiling sound immediately after turning off an internal combustion engine, it usually signals one of two things: active overheating while running, or residual heat causing thermal expansion and vaporization once the cooling system stops circulating. In your specific case with the 2000 Chrysler 300m, the combination of a recent loss of power, coolant depletion requiring four cups to refill, and immediate re-boiling points toward a catastrophic failure in the sealing integrity between the engine block and the radiator cap/overflow system.

The fact that the car required nearly two liters of water suggests you are losing more than just air pockets; the head gasket is likely compromised. When an engine overheats severely—enough to cause stalling and loss of power—the aluminum or iron cylinder heads can warp, or the gaskets between the block and heads can blow. This breach allows combustion gases under high pressure (often 150–200 PSI) to leak directly into the cooling system.

When you shut off the engine, the water pump stops pumping. Without that forced circulation, any trapped air pockets in the coolant will rise rapidly due to gravity and thermal expansion. If there is a head gasket leak, those escaping combustion gases expand as they hit the cooler temperatures of the coolant. This rapid expansion creates the "boiling" sound you heard even though the engine was off. The pressure forces the liquid out through the overflow reservoir or into the atmosphere if the cap is faulty, resulting in the massive loss of fluid you observed.

The previous diagnosis of a failing water pump and timing belt might have been secondary to the primary issue. While a seized water pump can certainly cause overheating by stopping circulation, it rarely explains the rapid coolant evaporation unless the pump housing itself cracked under extreme thermal stress. More commonly, a bad water pump leads to localized hot spots that eventually destroy the head gasket. The "nasty" water reported by your mechanic likely contained oil (from the crankcase breather leaking through a blown gasket) or excessive sludge from prolonged overheating, which can clog the radiator and heater core.

To verify this diagnosis without immediately tearing down the engine, you can perform a few non-invasive checks. Start with a combustion gas test on the coolant. Using a simple chemical test kit available at auto parts stores, you draw a sample of the remaining coolant from the overflow tank. If the solution changes color or indicates the presence of hydrocarbons, it confirms exhaust gases are in the radiator. This is a definitive sign that the head gasket is blown and will not hold pressure once the engine reaches operating temperature again.

Another method involves checking for external leaks while the engine is warm but off. Place cardboard under the vehicle and start the car to bring it up to temperature. Watch specifically at the base of the radiator, the thermostat housing, and the oil filler cap. Oil mixed with coolant often creates a chocolate milkshake appearance in the overflow tank or a white, powdery residue on the exhaust tailpipe.

If you proceed with repairs, replacing just the water pump is insufficient if the head gasket has failed. You must replace the gaskets (and potentially machine the heads to remove warping). The trade-off here is cost versus reliability; attempting to run an engine with a blown head gasket will result in warped valves, melted pistons, or complete engine seizure within hours.
